claims.text: Similarly, Lassila et al. (2025) develop BASE and G-BASE, tractable approximations of Bayes-optimal membership inference that match or exceed prior state-of-the-art performance at significantly lower computational cost.

Wu et al. (2024) address scalability from a measurement perspective, proposing a discrepancy-based privacy metric that does not require training multiple models and can be applied to large ImageNet classification models in-the-wild.
Naseh et al. (2025) present the first stealthy membership inference attack targeting RAG datastores, crafting natural-text queries that remain answerable only when the target document is present.

Emelyanov et al. (2025) extend perturbation-based membership inference to multimodal large language models, addressing the instabilities introduced through multimodal component adaptation and distribution shifts.

Zhu et al. (2025) tackle visual self-supervised models in realistic black-box settings where training paradigms and implementation details are unknown, proposing PartCrop which exploits shared part-aware capabilities across different self-supervised learning approaches.

Lassila et al. (2025) derive the Bayes-optimal membership inference rule for node-level attacks against graph neural networks, showing that BASE and the prior RMIA attack are equivalent under specific hyperparameter settings—providing a principled justification for existing methods.

Suri et al. (2024) provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that black-box access is insufficient for optimal membership inference when models are trained with stochastic gradient descent, establishing that white-box access to model parameters is necessary for optimal attacks.
Tao and Shokri (2024) introduce Range Membership Inference Attacks (RaMIAs) that test whether a model was trained on any data within a specified semantic range, rather than exact matches.

Wu et al. (2024) propose a discrepancy-based metric that upper-bounds the advantage of a family of membership inference attacks, providing theoretical guarantees on privacy leakage without requiring multiple model training.
Galichin et al. (2024) propose GLiRA, exploiting the connection between vulnerability to distillation-based functionality stealing and susceptibility to membership inference.
Du et al. (2025), Lassila et al. (2025), and Wu et al. (2024) all demonstrate that their methods achieve superior or comparable performance with dramatically reduced computational requirements.

There is also broad agreement that traditional black-box assumptions are insufficient—Suri et al. (2024) prove white-box access is theoretically necessary for optimal inference, while multiple papers develop methods that exploit additional information sources.
Similarly, white-box methods (Suri et al., 2024) and black-box methods (Galichin et al., 2024) address different adversary capabilities rather than contradicting each other.

Defense evaluation is limited: While Zhu et al. (2025) evaluate defenses including early stopping, differential privacy, and shrinking crop scale range, most papers focus on attack development without comprehensive defense analysis.
Galichin et al. (2024) note their evaluation is limited to image classification and may not generalize to NLP or tabular data.

Real-world deployment constraints: Several papers acknowledge their methods were tested on toy encoders or small-scale datasets (Zhu et al., 2025), with scaling studies being relatively recent additions.

Multimodal-specific challenges: Emelyanov et al. (2025) identify distribution shifts in multimodal datasets affecting MIA performance, but the framework's performance on unseen modalities and sensitivity to perturbation strategies remain open questions.
Parameter access assumptions: Suri et al. (2024) advocate for white-box methods but acknowledge that parameter access may not be available in many practical scenarios.
Research question: How can privacy risk measurement be improved beyond exact-match membership inference to capture privacy leakage from similar or partially overlapping memorized data?

Methodology: The authors introduce Range Membership Inference Attacks (RaMIAs) that test whether a model was trained on any data within a specified semantic range, formulating a principled statistical test for the composite hypotheses involved.
RaMIAs capture privacy loss more accurately and comprehensively than standard membership inference attacks
The approach works across various data types including tabular, image, and language data
RaMIAs enable more meaningful privacy auditing of machine learning algorithms
Similar or partially overlapping memorized data can reveal the same private information as exact matches
Limitations: The effectiveness of RaMIAs depends on appropriately defining ranges based on the semantics of privacy for each application domain.
